## Security scan

Every third-party skill above was scanned with [NVIDIA SkillSpector](https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector)
(static, 2026-10-04; animate-expo, ask-sonner, write-swift 2026-10-09 — all LOW, no HIGH) and each HIGH finding reviewed by hand. All were pattern matches on benign
text — anti-injection rules ("ignore previous instructions → flag it") read as overrides, HTML
template markers and zero-width spaces nesting code fences read as hidden text, "incomplete
analysis" of referenced files. No exfiltration, credential access, obfuscation or unverified
downloads (Impeccable's launcher checks its engine's sha256). Its every-edit hooks were not
installed.

### Official vendor skills (2026-11-25)

Scanned with SkillSpector 2.12.0 (static, `--no-llm`) from the pinned sources, and the final kit
copies again. All HIGH/CRITICAL findings were reviewed in context and are benign:
"incomplete analysis" of large referenced files; security references full of example attacks
(`rm -rf /`, `/etc/passwd`, `curl … | sh`, PHP webshells in sharp-edges and agentic-actions-auditor,
read as the real thing); setup steps that look for a token in `.env` / `VERCEL_TOKEN` and hand it to
the vendor CLI only (vercel-cli-with-tokens; note it prints the token into the chat); "access token"
wording in Supabase and Cloudflare docs; `os.environ.copy()` to start LibreOffice or a nested
`claude -p`; `shell=True` for the person's own dev-server command (webapp-testing);
`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in React examples; HTML comments in spec-kit templates. No hidden
Unicode (only byte-order marks in OOXML schemas and an emoji joiner), no bundled binaries, no
hooks. Network calls: supply-chain-risk-auditor queries public registries (OSV, npm, PyPI,
Go proxy, deps.dev, GitHub, OpenSSF Scorecard); deploy-to-vercel runs the Vercel CLI with npx (patched locally from `vercel@latest` to the pinned `vercel@66.6.0`, which the `/deploy` playbook uses too).

Not taken: `anthropics/skills` `brand-guidelines` (it applies Anthropic's own brand, wrong for
people's projects) and `web-artifacts-builder` (ships a `.tar.gz` the text-only kit packer can't
carry; builds claude.ai artifacts).

**skill-creator `eval-viewer` — patched locally** (security review, 2026-11-25): `generate_review.py`
escapes the embedded JSON for a `<script>` context (`<`, `>`, `&`, U+2028/2029 — eval output could
otherwise break out of the script); its local review server answers only requests whose Host and
Origin are `localhost`/`127.0.0.1` and saves feedback only with `Content-Type: application/json`
(no cross-site or DNS-rebinding writes); `viewer.html`'s `escapeHtml` also escapes quotes, as its
output is used inside `title="…"` attributes. Each change is marked "Ninja Builder patch".

# Connectors

This plugin uses three MCP connectors. All are optional — the pipeline runs in degraded mode without any of them.

---

## Ahrefs (primary — Stage 2)

**What it enables:**
- Jaccard similarity scoring for entity validation
- "Also Talk About" term retrieval for central keyword and all candidate entities
- Parent topic matching for proximity override
- Keyword volume + difficulty data for EAV model construction
- SERP overview for top-ranking page identification (feeds competitor context to Stage 3)

**To configure:** Connect your Ahrefs account in the Cowork connectors panel. Default endpoint: `https://api.ahrefs.com/mcp/mcp`.

**Without it:** Stage 2 runs in degraded mode. All entities are classified using domain knowledge only. No Jaccard scores. All entities marked "Unscored — manual review required". The rest of the pipeline continues normally.

**Ahrefs tools used:**
- `keywords-explorer-related-terms` (ATT retrieval — core of Stage 2)
- `keywords-explorer-overview` (volume / KD data for top entities)
- `serp-overview` (optional — competitor page identification)

---

## Google Drive

**What it enables:**
- Read editorial policies directly from shared Drive folders — no copy-pasting required
- Read project context files (context.json, dossier.md) for target audience, tone, and client rules
- Save finished articles, content briefs, QA reports, and pipeline reports to the correct client folder automatically

**To configure:** Connect your Google account in the Cowork connectors panel.

**Without it:** Paste the editorial policy directly into the chat. Save outputs manually. Project context must be pasted or described.

**Recommended folder structure:**
```
Content/
└── Clients/
    └── [Client Name]/
        ├── context.json          ← project context (audience, tone, brand rules)
        ├── dossier.md            ← extended project dossier
        ├── editorial-policy.md   ← editorial policy
        ├── briefs/
        │   └── [slug]-brief.md
        └── articles/
            └── [slug]-final.md
```

---

## Asana

**What it enables:**
- Create a review task when the pipeline completes and the article is ready for editorial review
- Assign the task to the right team member
- Include pipeline report summary in the task description

**To configure:** Connect your Asana account in the Cowork connectors panel. Default endpoint: `https://mcp.asana.com/sse`.

**Without it:** Pipeline completes normally. Task creation step is skipped with a prompt to create manually.

---

## Degraded mode reference

| Connector | Stage affected | Degraded behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Ahrefs | Stage 2 | Domain-knowledge classification only. No J scores. |
| Google Drive | All | Manual paste / manual save. |
| Asana | After Stage 6 | Task creation skipped. Manual reminder output. |

## Web access (built-in)

Stage 5 Agent C (fact-check) and Agent D (ai-citation-qa) use Claude's built-in web search / web fetch to verify claims against live primary sources. No connector setup required.

# Content Pipeline Plugin v4.0

Full end-to-end SEO content pipeline. Input a keyword + GEO. Get a publication-ready, QA-verified article. **Fully self-contained — all 6 stages and all skills are inside this single zip.**

**v4.0 is a tuning release for Claude Opus 5.** Same six stages, same methodology, materially faster and more accurate:

- **File-based handoffs.** Every stage writes an artifact and prints a short receipt. Previously each stage's full output was printed into chat and re-pasted downstream, so a brief and an article each appeared in context three or four times. Now the next stage reads the file.
- **Jaccard is computed in code, not in-head.** ~1,000 string comparisons per run used to be done mentally, producing scores that were approximately right — fatal for threshold-based tier classification. A script now produces exact values.
- **Parallel tool calls.** Candidate ATT lookups, keyword overviews, pre-writing research and fact-check source fetches are all batched into single messages instead of issued one at a time.
- **QA reviewers detect exhaustively, then classify.** Opus 5 follows conservative review instructions literally and reports less. Severity language was rewritten so calibration no longer runs during detection.
- **No over-verification.** Opus 5 checks its own work unprompted. Pre-output self-verify checklists were converted to hard constraints stated once, which removes a redundant pass per stage without loss of quality.
- **Delegation capped.** Stage 5 is the only stage that delegates, exactly four subagents, once. Each reviewer is explicitly a leaf agent.
- **Resumable across sessions.** Because state lives on disk rather than in the transcript, a run survives an interruption, a context reset, or a brand new conversation.

---

## Pipeline stages

| Stage | Name | Skill | Writes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Query Fan-Out | `skills/fan-out-adapter/` | `01-fanout.md` |
| 2 | Ahrefs Entity Research (Jaccard) | `skills/ahrefs-entity-research/` | `02-entities.md`, `02-jaccard.json` |
| 3 | Content Guidelines | `skills/content-guidelines/` | `03-brief.md` |
| 4 | Content Generation | `skills/content-generation/` | `04-draft.md` |
| 5 | Quad QA — 4 parallel reviewers | `skills/quad-qa/` | `05-qa-*.md` |
| 6 | Revision & Final Draft | (uses quad-qa unified fix list) | `06-final.md`, `06-revision-log.md` |

Artifacts land in `outputs/pipeline/[date]-[keyword-slug]/`.

### The four QA reviewers

| Agent | Checks | Gate output |
|---|---|---|
| A — Editorial QA | Editorial policy compliance | Critical/Major/Minor |
| B — SEO Brief QA | Brief compliance: structure, entities, EAV, fan-out | Critical/Major/Minor |
| C — Fact-Check | Every claim vs primary sources | Claims ledger + PASS/FAIL |
| D — AI Citation QA | LLM retrievability: chunk self-containment, EAV precision, intent-format match, extractable structures, E-E-A-T distribution | Citation Readiness Score /100 |

Combined gate: **❌ BLOCKED / ⚠️ REVISE / ✅ CLEARED**. Conflict precedence: Fact-Check > Editorial policy > SEO brief > AI citation.

Stage 6 states its post-revision gate as **projected**, not measured — it fixes the findings and reports which it closed, rather than re-running four reviewers on every pass. Run `/pipeline:qa` when you need a measured gate.

---

## Slash commands

| Command | When to use |
|---|---|
| `/pipeline:run` | Full 6-stage pipeline — keyword → final article. The primary command. |
| `/pipeline:qa` | Re-run Quad QA against an existing article. Verifies a Stage 6 revision, or QAs any outside draft. |
| `/pipeline:status` | Check progress from artifacts on disk, resume from any stage |
| `/pipeline:entities` | Run Stage 2 (Ahrefs Jaccard entity scoring) in isolation |

---

## What you need to start

Just two things:

1. **Keyword / Topic** — e.g. `"BPC-157 peptide therapy"`, `"sweepstakes casino no deposit bonus"`
2. **Target Country / GEO** — e.g. `"United States"`, `"Australia"`

Everything else (audience, purpose, competitor structure, LSI terms) is resolved from project context or inferred. Missing competitor page text no longer stalls Stage 3 — it falls back to ATT-derived structure and labels the brief accordingly.

---

## Effort calibration

Opus 5 produces strong quality at `low` and `medium` effort at a fraction of the tokens, so effort is the primary cost lever. Calibrated per stage:

| Stage | Effort | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 — Fan-Out | `medium` | Structured decomposition, little deep reasoning |
| 2 — Entity Research | `medium` | Tool calls plus a script; the arithmetic is not yours |
| 3 — Content Guidelines | `high` | Synthesis across entities, intents and competitor gaps |
| 4 — Content Generation | `high` (`xhigh` for YMYL) | The stage where quality is actually created |
| 5 — Quad QA | `medium` | Review precision holds at lower effort |
| 6 — Revision | `high` | Targeted edits under a precedence chain |

Re-run an effort sweep on your own outputs before settling — these are starting points, not measurements of your niche.

**Optional cost routing.** Agents A and B match content against a supplied document, which holds up on a smaller model. C and D do live source verification and retrievability judgment; keep those at full strength. Keep all four at full strength for YMYL.

---

## The entity research methodology (Stage 2)

Stage 2 uses **Jaccard similarity on Ahrefs "Also Talk About" (ATT) data** as a semantic proximity signal — the closest available proxy to real cosine similarity without running embeddings.

**Formula:**
```
J(central, candidate) = |ATT_central ∩ ATT_candidate| / |ATT_central ∪ ATT_candidate|
```

**Computed in code.** The skill carries a script that normalizes both term sets identically (lowercase, collapse whitespace, dedupe), computes exact intersection and union, applies thresholds, and writes `02-jaccard.json`. Every number in the report is read from that file. This is not a convenience — tier classification is threshold-based, so an approximate J score silently misclassifies entities.

**Default thresholds:**

| J score | Tier | Article treatment |
|---|---|---|
| ≥ 0.15 OR parent topic match | High proximity | Primary entity — dedicated H2 section |
| ≥ 0.05 | Medium proximity | Supporting entity — subsection or inline |
| < 0.05 | Low proximity | Contextual mention only, or exclude |

**Parent topic override:** a candidate sharing Ahrefs' `parent_topic` with the central keyword is High regardless of J score — a direct signal that one page tends to rank for both. Overrides are individually flagged so a High tier is never mistaken for a high J score.

**Calibration:** thresholds are educated starting points. Every run emits calibration notes in the revision log. Lower them (High ≥ 0.10, Medium ≥ 0.03) for tight niches with small ATT sets.

---

## Plugin structure

```
content-pipeline/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
├── commands/
│   ├── run.md              ← /pipeline:run       (full pipeline)
│   ├── qa.md               ← /pipeline:qa        (re-run Quad QA)
│   ├── status.md           ← /pipeline:status    (resume from artifacts)
│   └── entities.md         ← /pipeline:entities  (Stage 2 only)
├── skills/
│   ├── fan-out-adapter/         ← Stage 1: sub-intent decomposition
│   ├── ahrefs-entity-research/  ← Stage 2: Jaccard scoring via Ahrefs MCP
│   ├── content-guidelines/      ← Stage 3: content brief with EAV + token budgets
│   ├── content-generation/      ← Stage 4: article writing
│   ├── quad-qa/                 ← Stage 5: parallel 4-reviewer orchestrator
│   ├── editorial-qa/            ← Stage 5, Agent A: editorial policy compliance
│   ├── seo-brief-qa/            ← Stage 5, Agent B: brief compliance
│   ├── fact-check/              ← Stage 5, Agent C: claims vs primary sources
│   └── ai-citation-qa/          ← Stage 5, Agent D: LLM retrievability & citability
├── CONNECTORS.md
└── README.md
```

No external dependencies. The `content-production` plugin is **not required**.

---

## Connectors

| Connector | Stage | What it enables | Required? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ahrefs MCP** | Stage 2 | Jaccard scoring, ATT retrieval, volume data | Recommended. Degrades gracefully without it. |
| **Google Drive** | All | Read editorial policies; save outputs | Optional |
| **Asana MCP** | After Stage 6 | Create review task on completion | Optional |

**Degraded mode:** without Ahrefs, Stage 2 runs on domain-knowledge classification (no J scores). All other stages are unaffected. The pipeline never stops for a missing connector.

---

## Upgrading from v3.0

Drop-in replacement — same commands, same methodology, no migration. Two behavioural changes to expect:

1. **Chat output is much shorter.** Stage outputs go to files; you get a receipt per stage. Review artifacts in the run directory rather than scrolling the transcript. The final article is presented as a file.
2. **Stage 6's gate is labelled projected.** v3.0 asserted `CLEARED` without re-measuring. v4.0 says so honestly and points at `/pipeline:qa` when you need a measured gate.

---

## Installation

Drop the `content-pipeline/` folder into your Cowork plugins directory. Restart Cowork. No other plugins required.

description: Run Ahrefs entity research (Jaccard similarity scoring) in isolation — without running the full pipeline. Use when you already have an entity list and want to validate and score it against a keyword.
---

# /pipeline:entities

Run Stage 2 (Ahrefs Entity Research) in isolation. Takes a keyword + candidate entity list and returns a Jaccard-scored, classified entity model ready to feed into content guidelines.

---

## Required inputs

1. **Central keyword** — the primary target keyword
2. **Target country / GEO** — used for Ahrefs country filter
3. **Candidate entity list** — the entities you want to validate (paste as a list)

Optional:
- **Similarity threshold override** — if you want to adjust the classification thresholds (default: J ≥ 0.15 → high proximity, J ≥ 0.05 → medium proximity)

---

## Execution

Apply `skills/ahrefs-entity-research/SKILL.md` in full. Two things that matter for speed and accuracy:

- **Batch the ATT calls.** All candidate lookups are independent — issue them in a single message.
- **Compute Jaccard in code**, per the script in the skill. Never estimate set overlap by reading the lists.

Write `02-entities.md` and `02-jaccard.json` to the outputs folder.

---

## Output

Print a receipt, not the report:

```
✅ Entity Research → 02-entities.md
[N] entities scored: [n] High · [n] Medium · [n] Low[ · [n] unscored]
ATT_central: [n] terms. Parent topic: [value]. Overrides: [n]
[N] ATT clusters → [n] uncovered (gaps flagged)
```

Then offer one next step: feed this into a content brief via `/pipeline:run` starting from Stage 3.

---
description: Run Quad QA (4 parallel reviewers) against an existing article without regenerating it. Use to verify a Stage 6 revision, or to QA any article written outside the pipeline.
---

# /pipeline:qa

Run all four QA reviewers against an article that already exists. No generation, no revision — review only.

---

## Two ways this gets used

**Verify a Stage 6 revision.** Stage 6 projects its gate rather than re-measuring it, because re-running four reviewers on every pass is expensive and usually redundant. When a measured gate actually matters — a client deliverable, a YMYL page, anything going out under someone's byline — run this against `06-final.md` to get the real number.

**QA an outside article.** Any draft, from any source. Supply what you have; the reviewers degrade gracefully around missing inputs.

---

## Inputs

| Input | Reviewer | If missing |
|---|---|---|
| Article (required) | all | Ask for it |
| Editorial policy | A — Editorial | Agent A skipped, gap noted |
| SEO content brief | B — SEO Brief | Agent B skipped, gap noted |
| Fan-out / sub-intents | D — AI Citation | Agent D infers intents from structure |

Fact-check (Agent C) always runs — it locates primary sources itself.

Inside a run directory these resolve automatically: `06-final.md` (or `04-draft.md`), `03-brief.md`, `01-fanout.md`. Only the editorial policy needs supplying if it was not provided at run time.

---

## Execution

Apply `skills/quad-qa/SKILL.md` in full: four reviewers dispatched as parallel subagents in a single message, each writing its own report, then deduplication, conflict resolution via the precedence chain, and a combined gate.

Verifying a revision: pass the previous `05-qa-consolidated.md` as well. quad-qa diffs against it, showing which violations closed and which survived — and a violation that survived a revision pass escalates one severity level.

Write reports to the run directory, suffixed to avoid overwriting the first pass:
`05b-qa-a-editorial.md` … `05b-qa-consolidated.md`

---

## Output

Lead with the gate. Then the scoreboard, then the file.

```
Gate: [❌ BLOCKED / ⚠️ REVISE / ✅ CLEARED] — [decisive factor]
🔴 [n] · 🟡 [n] · 🟠 [n]  |  Fact-check: [PASS/FAIL]  |  Citation: [n]/100
[If diffing: closed [n] · persisted [n] (escalated) · new [n]]
→ 05b-qa-consolidated.md
```

If the gate is not CLEARED, offer one next step: revise against the unified fix list.

---
description: Full 6-stage content pipeline from keyword to publication-ready article. Input a keyword/topic + target country. Claude runs everything autonomously — fan-out, entity research via Ahrefs Jaccard scoring, content guidelines, content generation, quad QA (4 parallel reviewers), and final revision producing the publication-ready draft.
---

# /pipeline:run

Run the complete content pipeline from a single keyword through to a publication-ready, QA-verified, revised article.

---

## Required inputs

Ask for these before starting. Do not proceed if either is missing.

1. **Keyword / Topic** — the primary target keyword or topic (e.g. "BPC-157 peptide therapy", "sweepstakes casino no deposit bonus", "GLP-1 weight loss injections")
2. **Target Country / GEO** — the target market (e.g. "United States", "United Kingdom", "Australia")

Optional — resolve these automatically if not provided:
- **Editorial policy** — paste, or point to a file/Drive path. If absent, ask once, then proceed without it and note the gap in the Stage 5 report.
- **Target audience** — inferred from keyword + project context.

---

## How this pipeline runs (read first)

**Artifacts, not transcripts.** Every stage writes its full output to a file in the run directory and prints a short receipt to chat. The next stage reads the file. Never paste a full stage output into chat "so the next stage can see it" — the next stage reads the path.

Create the run directory before Stage 1:

```
outputs/pipeline/[YYYY-MM-DD]-[keyword-slug]/
├── 01-fanout.md
├── 02-entities.md
├── 02-jaccard.json
├── 03-brief.md
├── 04-draft.md
├── 05-qa-a-editorial.md
├── 05-qa-b-seo-brief.md
├── 05-qa-c-fact-check.md
├── 05-qa-d-ai-citation.md
├── 05-qa-consolidated.md
├── 06-final.md
└── 06-revision-log.md
```

**Stage receipt format.** After each stage, print only this — nothing else:

```
✅ Stage [N] — [Name] → [filename]
[3–5 lines: the numbers that matter for the next stage and any degradations]
```

**Autonomy.** Run all 6 stages in order without stopping. The only pauses: (a) before Stage 1 if a required input is missing, (b) after Stage 6 to offer saving/handoff. Do not ask for confirmation between stages.

**Degradation never stops the run.** If Ahrefs MCP is unavailable, note it in the Stage 2 receipt and continue in domain-knowledge mode. Same for any other missing connector.

---

## Execution discipline

Deliver what was asked, at the scope intended. Make routine judgment calls yourself and check in only when two readings of the request would produce materially different articles. If a stage input looks wrong or a better approach exists, say so in one sentence and continue with the pipeline as specified rather than quietly redesigning it. Finish all six stages; stop short of work beyond them.

**Narration.** Before Stage 1, say in one sentence what you are about to do. After that, speak only through stage receipts, plus a brief line if you find something that changes the plan (Ahrefs empty, editorial policy contradicts the brief, fact-check blocks publication). Do not announce what you are about to do before each stage — the receipt after it is enough.

**Corrections.** Only flag a correction to something you said earlier when it would change the article or the user's decision. Otherwise fix it silently and continue.

---
name: ahrefs-entity-research
description: >
  Validates and scores candidate entities for a target keyword using Ahrefs "Also Talk About" (ATT)
  data and Jaccard similarity coefficients as a semantic proximity proxy. Classifies entities into
  high / medium / low proximity tiers, builds EAV models for top entities, and produces a structured
  report ready to feed the Content Guidelines stage. Use this skill whenever entity validation
  via real Ahrefs co-occurrence data is needed — either as Stage 2 of the full pipeline or
  as a standalone entity scoring run. Requires Ahrefs MCP connection.
---

# Ahrefs Entity Research — Jaccard Similarity Scoring

You are an SEO entity analyst. Your job is to validate and score a list of candidate entities against a central keyword using Ahrefs "Also Talk About" (ATT) co-occurrence data as a semantic proximity signal. You will compute Jaccard similarity coefficients, classify entities by proximity tier, and build an EAV model for the top-scoring entities.

---

## What this is — and isn't

This is **not** cosine similarity. This is **Jaccard similarity** applied to ATT keyword sets as a semantic proximity proxy.

**The formula:**

```
J(central, candidate) = |ATT_central ∩ ATT_candidate| / |ATT_central ∪ ATT_candidate|
```

Where:
- `ATT_central` = the set of "Also Talk About" terms for the central keyword
- `ATT_candidate` = the set of "Also Talk About" terms for the candidate entity keyword
- Intersection = terms appearing in BOTH sets
- Union = all unique terms across both sets

**Jaccard values tend to be low** for large ATT sets. A 15% overlap (J = 0.15) is a strong co-occurrence signal. Do not interpret low Jaccard scores as weak signals without context.

---

## Non-negotiable: compute Jaccard in code, never in your head

Set intersection and union across ~100-term lists for 10 candidates is ~1,000 string comparisons. Doing it mentally is slower than running it and produces scores that are approximately right, which is worse than useless for tier classification. **Write the ATT sets to JSON and run the script.**

The workflow is: collect raw ATT terms → write JSON → run script → read exact scores → interpret. You do the interpretation. The machine does the arithmetic.

Normalization matters and is easy to get wrong by hand — the script handles it: lowercase, strip surrounding whitespace, collapse internal whitespace, drop empty strings, deduplicate. Apply it identically to both sets, always.

---

## Inputs

Confirm you have these before starting. If any are missing, ask:

1. **Central keyword** — the primary target keyword (e.g. "sweepstakes casino")
2. **Target country / GEO** — Ahrefs country code (e.g. "us", "gb", "au")
3. **Candidate entity list** — list of 5–15 entities to validate (from Stage 1 fan-out handoff or user-provided)
4. **Similarity thresholds** — use defaults unless user overrides:
   - J ≥ 0.15 → **High proximity** (same article — treat as primary entity)
   - J ≥ 0.05 → **Medium proximity** (supporting section — include as supporting entity)
   - J < 0.05 → **Low proximity** (contextual mention only — include briefly or omit)

---

## Process

Execute these phases in order. Use Ahrefs MCP throughout.

---

### Phase 1: Central Keyword ATT Retrieval

Call Ahrefs `keywords-explorer-related-terms` for the central keyword:

```
tool: Ahrefs:keywords-explorer-related-terms
params:
  keyword: [central keyword]
  country: [GEO code]
  terms: "also_talk_about"
  limit: 100
```

Store the full ATT term list as `ATT_central`. Log the count (typically 60–100 terms).

Also retrieve the `parent_topic` for the central keyword. Note it — a shared parent topic with a candidate is a direct ≥0.85 proximity signal (maps to High tier regardless of Jaccard score).

---

### Phase 2: Candidate ATT Retrieval — issue all calls in parallel

Every candidate needs the same call, and none of them depend on each other. **Issue all candidate ATT calls in a single message** so they resolve concurrently. Ten sequential round-trips is ten times the latency for identical results.

```
tool: Ahrefs:keywords-explorer-related-terms
params:
  keyword: [candidate entity]
  country: [GEO code]
  terms: "also_talk_about"
  limit: 100
```

Also capture each candidate's `parent_topic` from the same response.

---

### Phase 3: Jaccard computation (in code)

Write the collected sets to `02-jaccard-input.json`:

```json
{
  "central": {"keyword": "...", "parent_topic": "...", "att": ["term", "term", "..."]},
  "candidates": [
    {"keyword": "...", "parent_topic": "...", "att": ["term", "..."]}
  ],
  "thresholds": {"high": 0.15, "medium": 0.05}
}
```

Run this script against it:

```python
import json, sys

def norm(terms):
    return {" ".join(t.lower().split()) for t in terms if t and t.strip()}

d = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
C = norm(d["central"]["att"])
cp = (d["central"].get("parent_topic") or "").strip().lower()
th = d.get("thresholds", {"high": 0.15, "medium": 0.05})
rows = []

for c in d["candidates"]:
    A = norm(c["att"])
    inter, union = C & A, C | A
    j = len(inter) / len(union) if union else 0.0
    pt = (c.get("parent_topic") or "").strip().lower()
    match = bool(cp) and pt == cp
    if not A:
        tier, note = "Unscored", "no ATT data returned"
    elif match:
        tier, note = "High", "parent topic override"
    elif j >= th["high"]:
        tier, note = "High", ""
    elif j >= th["medium"]:
        tier, note = "Medium", ""
    else:
        tier, note = "Low", ""
    rows.append({
        "entity": c["keyword"], "att_size": len(A),
        "intersection": len(inter), "union": len(union),
        "jaccard": round(j, 4), "parent_topic_match": match,
        "tier": tier, "note": note,
        "shared_terms": sorted(inter)[:25],
    })

rows.sort(key=lambda r: (-r["parent_topic_match"], -r["jaccard"]))
out = {
    "central_att_size": len(C),
    "central_parent_topic": d["central"].get("parent_topic"),
    "thresholds": th,
    "tier_counts": {t: sum(1 for r in rows if r["tier"] == t)
                    for t in ("High", "Medium", "Low", "Unscored")},
    "results": rows,
    "uncovered_central_terms": sorted(
        C - set().union(*[norm(c["att"]) for c in d["candidates"]] or [set()])
    ),
}
json.dump(out, open("02-jaccard.json", "w"), indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
print(json.dumps({k: out[k] for k in
      ("central_att_size", "central_parent_topic", "tier_counts")}, ensure_ascii=False))
for r in rows:
    print(f"{r['tier']:9} J={r['jaccard']:.4f}  {r['intersection']:>3}/{r['union']:<4} "
          f"pt={'Y' if r['parent_topic_match'] else 'N'}  {r['entity']} {r['note']}")
```

Read the exact scores from `02-jaccard.json`. Every number in your report comes from that file — do not re-derive, round differently, or eyeball any of it.

`uncovered_central_terms` is the raw material for Phase 6 gap analysis: central ATT terms no candidate touches.

**Parent topic override rule:** a candidate sharing the central keyword's parent topic is **High proximity** regardless of J score — Ahrefs is telling you directly that one page tends to rank for both. The script applies this; flag each override in the report so the reader knows the tier did not come from J.

---

### Phase 4: Keyword Overview for High + Medium entities

Pull volume, KD, CPC and SERP features for every High and Medium entity. These calls are also independent — **batch them in one message**.

```
tool: Ahrefs:keywords-explorer-overview
params:
  keyword: [candidate entity]
  country: [GEO code]
```

The `shared_terms` array already in `02-jaccard.json` gives you each entity's semantic bridge to the central keyword. Those terms become LSI context words, EAV attribute candidates, and internal linking anchors — take the top 10 per entity from the file.

---

### Phase 5: EAV Model Construction

For each High proximity entity, build an EAV model with 3–5 attribute-value pairs. Source attributes from:
- Shared ATT terms (high-volume shared terms become attributes)
- Ahrefs keyword overview data (volume, difficulty → quantitative values)
- Domain knowledge (standard attributes for this entity type in this niche)

For each Medium proximity entity, build a minimal EAV with 2–3 attributes.

---

### Phase 6: Semantic Gap Discovery

This phase is judgment, not arithmetic — it is yours to do, not the script's.

1. Take `uncovered_central_terms` from `02-jaccard.json`: central ATT terms no candidate entity touches. These are the raw signal for **missing entity gaps**.
2. Cluster the full `ATT_central` set into 3–5 thematic groups. These clusters map to the article's H2 structure.
3. Flag any cluster with no candidate entity covering it, and recommend the entity that would cover it.

---

## Output Format

Write the full report to `02-entities.md` in the run directory (standalone runs: the outputs folder). Print only a short receipt to chat — tier counts, ATT_central size, parent topic, cluster gaps, and any degradation. Do not print the report body.

No preamble in the file — it opens on the H1.

## Hard requirements

These are constraints on the report, not a checklist to run afterwards. The report is wrong if any is false:

- Every number in the report is read from `02-jaccard.json`, not recomputed.
- Every candidate that returned ATT data appears in the scoring table, including Low tier.
- Every High entity has a 3–5 attribute EAV model; every Medium entity has 2–3.
- H2 recommendations derive from **ATT clusters**, not from the candidate list. The clusters are the signal the candidates were meant to test.
- Parent-topic overrides are individually flagged, so a High tier is never mistaken for a high J score.

---

## Error Handling

**If Ahrefs returns no ATT data for a candidate entity:**
- Note it in the table: "No ATT data — entity may be too niche or too broad for this keyword in this GEO"
- Do not compute Jaccard — mark as "Unscored"
- Apply domain knowledge to classify manually and note it

**If Ahrefs ATT sets are very small (<20 terms):**
- Note the limitation in the output
- Jaccard scores will be less reliable — apply lower confidence to tier classification
- Supplement with `keywords-explorer-related-terms` using `terms: "also_rank_for"` as a fallback

**If Ahrefs MCP is unavailable:**
- Flag clearly: "Ahrefs MCP not connected — running in degraded mode"
- Fall back to domain-knowledge entity classification (no Jaccard scoring)
- Mark all entities as "Unscored — manual review required"
- Continue pipeline — do not block

---

## Pipeline Context

This skill is Stage 2 of the 6-stage content pipeline:

1. **Query Fan-Out** → 10 sub-intents + candidate entity list → `01-fanout.md`
2. **Ahrefs Entity Research** (this skill) → Jaccard scoring, tiers, EAV models → `02-entities.md` + `02-jaccard.json`
3. **Content Guidelines** → sub-intents + scored entities → content brief → `03-brief.md`
4. **Content Generation** → the article → `04-draft.md`
5. **Quad QA** → editorial + SEO brief + fact-check + AI citation, in parallel → `05-*.md`
6. **Revision** → publication-ready draft → `06-final.md`

Stage 3 reads the "Pipeline Handoff" section of `02-entities.md` directly from the file. Write it complete and self-contained; do not paste it into chat.

---
name: ai-citation-qa
description: The fourth QA reviewer in the content pipeline — evaluates whether an article is optimized for retrieval and citation by AI systems (Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude). Checks passage self-containment, entity clarity, EAV precision, intent-format match, extractable structures, evidence-backed claims, freshness, and E-E-A-T signal distribution. Produces a Citation Readiness Score (0–100), severity-classified violations (Critical/Major/Minor), and a PASS/FAIL gate. Use whenever an article needs LLM-extractability review, GEO/AEO QA, AI citation audit, or as QA Agent D alongside editorial-qa, seo-brief-qa, and fact-check. Trigger on "citation QA", "AI citation check", "LLM optimization check", "GEO QA", "extractability audit", "will AI cite this", or any pre-publish QA request where AI visibility matters.
---

# AI Citation QA Skill

You are an AI-retrievability quality analyst. Your sole function is to evaluate whether a completed article will be **retrieved, extracted, and cited by AI answer engines** — Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude. You do not rewrite content and you do not evaluate editorial tone, brief compliance, or factual truth — those belong to editorial-qa, seo-brief-qa, and fact-check respectively.

**The core premise you evaluate against:** AI systems do not use whole documents. They chunk content, embed the chunks, and rank at the **passage level**. A passage wins citation when it is a complete, self-contained, precisely-worded answer to a specific sub-intent. Your job is to find every passage that fails this test and every structural choice that lowers retrievability.

Report in the same language as the article (Russian article → Russian report).

## Step 0 — Input check

Required:
- **Article** — the completed content to evaluate.

Optional (use when present, degrade gracefully when absent):
- **Content brief / fan-out output** — gives you the sub-intent list. Without it, infer the central intent and sub-intents from the article's H1/H2 structure and note that you did.
- **Target query/keyword** — helps classify the dominant intent type.

If the article is missing, respond only with: "Please provide the article to evaluate."

## Step 1 — Intent classification

Classify the dominant intent of the article and of each H2 section. This determines the expected answer format:

| Intent type | Query pattern | Expected content format |
|---|---|---|
| Transactional | "best [product]", "top [service]" | Ranked list with specific recommendations |
| Informational | "what is [X]", "how does [X] work" | Definition + mechanism explanation |
| Comparative | "[A] vs [B]", "which is better" | Side-by-side comparison table |
| Navigational | "[brand] [feature]" | Direct answer about the specific entity |
| Trust/Safety | "is [X] safe", "is [X] legit" | Credibility signals + verification criteria |
| Tactical | "how to [outcome]" | Step-by-step process or priority actions |
| Troubleshooting | "why isn't [X] working" | Problem–solution pairs |

**Format-mismatch check:** a section whose intent is Comparative but contains no table, or Tactical with no numbered steps, is a violation — AI systems select the content whose format already matches the answer shape they want to produce.

**One intent per H2.** A section that mixes two or more intent clusters splits its embedding and loses to competitors' single-intent sections. Flag every mixed-intent H2.

## Step 2 — Evaluation areas

### Area 1 — Passage self-containment (the chunk test)

For each paragraph, ask: **could this paragraph be lifted out alone and serve as a complete answer to some sub-intent, with zero surrounding context?**

Self-containment checklist per paragraph:
- Entity named explicitly (not "it", "this", "they", "этот сервис", "она")
- Values specified (not "more", "better", "significantly improved" — actual numbers)
- Context included (no "as mentioned above", "как мы уже говорили")
- Complete thought (does not require prior sentences to parse)

Also check paragraph mechanics:
- Opens with the main claim (BLUF — the first sentence must be extractable as the answer)
- 2–4 sentences, one sub-intent per paragraph
- Closes with a concrete reader benefit or a bridge to the next idea

**Anaphora audit:** count pronoun-subject sentences ("It also offers…", "They provide…"). Every sentence whose grammatical subject is a pronoun referring to an entity in a *previous* paragraph is a broken chunk boundary.

### Area 2 — Entity clarity & terminology consistency

- **Named entities over generic nouns.** "Google Search Console", not "this tool". Brands, people, products, places resolve meaning for the model.
- **One term per concept, used consistently.** Synonym rotation ("платформа" → "сервис" → "решение" for the same product) weakens the entity embedding. Repetition of the precise term strengthens it. Flag concepts referred to by 3+ different terms.
- **Modifiers and descriptors.** "Enterprise SEO agency" carries more meaning than "agency". Flag key entities that appear repeatedly without differentiating qualifiers where similar entities could be confused.

### Area 3 — EAV precision

AI systems prioritize content with clean Entity–Attribute–Value structure.

- Bad: "This casino has a great welcome bonus with lots of coins."
- Good: "Playtana awards 125,000 GC + 1.00 SC upon registration with email verification required."
- Template: **"[Entity] offers [specific feature] at [exact value] with [quantifiable benefit]."**

For every significant claim, verify the triplet is complete and diagnose the broken element exactly as seo-brief-qa does: **entity unnamed / attribute vague / value absent**. (Scope note: seo-brief-qa checks EAV against the brief's entity list; you check EAV as a retrievability property across the whole article — every claim, whether briefed or not.)

**Superlative backing:** AI engines prefer unambiguous answers to "best/top/highest" queries, but only when the claim carries its evidence in the same sentence. Template: "[Entity] represents the [superlative claim] with [supporting metric]." Every unbacked superlative is a violation — it lowers the authority of the whole document.

**Vague-quantifier audit:** flag "many", "several", "a lot", "widely", "значительно", "множество" wherever a number could exist.

### Area 4 — Structured formats & extractability

Structured data is extracted 3–4× more often for comparison-type queries.

| Content type | Required format |
|---|---|
| Feature comparisons | Comparison table (entity names in FIRST column, ≤7 rows) |
| Specifications | Attribute table |
| Pricing tiers | Pricing table |
| Process steps | Numbered list |
| Requirements/criteria | Bulleted list |
| Pros and cons | Two-column table |

- Minimum one structured element (list or table) per ~300 words of prose. Count and flag deficits.
- Comparison tables placed as early as possible within their section.
- Tables longer than 7 rows should be split or trimmed — long tables chunk badly.

### Area 5 — FAQ quality

If the article has a FAQ (and for most informational/comparative pieces it should — FAQ maps directly onto People Also Ask and fan-out sub-queries):

- Each question phrased naturally AND containing the entity (not "Is it safe?" but "Is Playtana safe?")
- Answer structure: **first sentence = direct answer; second sentence = one specific datapoint; optional third = exception, condition, or next step**
- 2–3 sentences per answer, each answer fully independent
- Flag answers that open with throat-clearing ("That's a great question worth exploring…") or restate the question

### Area 6 — Semantic chunking & document architecture

- H2 sections: one intent each, 150–400 words. Over 300 words → must have H3 subdivisions.
- Clean heading hierarchy H1 → H2 → H3, no skipped levels.
- Headings phrased as retrievable queries or entity+attribute statements — a heading is the chunk's strongest retrieval hook. "Дозировка BPC-157" beats "Что нужно знать".
- Highest-priority content at the top of the document. The first 100 words after H1 must contain a direct, self-contained answer to the central intent (the "answer capsule"). This is the single most-cited passage pattern across AI engines.
- Document ends with a summary that restates key extractable claims (a second citation surface for the same facts).

### Area 7 — Content priority matrix

Estimate the share of text by priority band:

| Priority | Criterion | Target share |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Direct answer to the central intent | 40–50% |
| P2 | Answers to sub-intents | 30–35% |
| P3 | Unique info competitors lack | 10–15% |
| P4 | Supporting context | 5–10% |
| P5 | History, tangents, filler | 0% |

Any P5 content is a violation. P1 below ~35% means the article is diluted — flag with the specific sections that should shrink.

### Area 8 — Freshness signals

- Year in title/H1 for annual or seasonal topics.
- "Last Updated" timestamp present for dynamic topics.
- Recent developments referenced where the topic moves fast; no timeless-sounding claims ("prices never change") on dynamic subjects.
- Undated statistics on time-sensitive claims — flag (fact-check verifies truth; you verify the *dating* is visible to the retrieval system).

### Area 9 — E-E-A-T signal distribution

Trust-adjacent queries require reliability signals distributed through the content, not quarantined in a disclaimer block.

| Signal | Form |
|---|---|
| Regulatory | Governing bodies, licenses, certifications |
| Expert | Named professionals, credentials, quotes |
| Data | Statistics from authoritative sources |
| Third-party | Independent reviews, ratings, audits |
| Institutional | Industry associations, standards bodies |
| Temporal | Publication dates, update timestamps |

- At least one authority signal per major section.
- Key signals near the top, reinforced in the conclusion.
- For Trust/Safety intent sections this is Critical, not Major.

**Verifiability sub-checks (weigh heavily on YMYL topics — health, finance, legal, safety):**
- **Sources resolvable, not just named.** "According to Cleveland Clinic" as plain text gives the retrieval system no citation graph. Sources must be linked (or clearly linkable). Named-but-unlinked sources on a YMYL topic = Critical.
- **Attribution near the claim.** A statistic whose source sits only in a footer source list is a weaker chunk than one carrying "по данным [source]" in the same passage — the passage is extracted alone, so its trust signals must travel with it. Flag key numbers whose attribution does not survive chunk extraction.
- **Named author / reviewer.** An anonymous "staff writer" or generic "врач клиники" byline on YMYL content suppresses citation versus competitors with a named, credentialed reviewer. Flag when the byline names no verifiable person.
- **Source-locale match.** All sources in a different language/market than the article's audience weakens authority legibility for that market. Flag as Minor.

### Area 10 — Citation-worthiness (why cite YOU)

An AI engine cites the source that gives it something specific to attribute. Assess:
- **Unique datapoint density** — original numbers, named tests, first-party data, proprietary comparisons. An article that only restates common knowledge gives the engine no reason to cite it over Wikipedia.
- **Quotable sentences** — at least a handful of sentences that work as standalone attributed quotes ("According to [site], …"). Sentences under ~25 words with entity + value are ideal quote candidates.
- **Anti-fluff:** flag rhetorical openers ("In today's fast-paced digital world…", "В современном мире…"), filler questions used as transitions, and paragraphs that delay the answer. These raise the cost of retrieval and push the real answer out of the chunk window.

## Severity classification

**Detect first, classify second.** Work all ten areas and log every retrievability defect before assigning severities. Ranking during detection suppresses findings. Anything you are unsure how to rank goes in as Minor — never omitted.

| Level | Definition |
|---|---|
| 🔴 Critical | No answer capsule in the first 100 words; central-intent H2 with mixed intents or wrong format (e.g., comparative intent with no table); primary claims with broken EAV; unbacked superlative on the central claim; E-E-A-T signals absent on Trust/Safety intent; named-but-unlinked sources or anonymous byline on YMYL content; P5 content over 5% of text. |
| 🟡 Major | Paragraph fails self-containment in a P1/P2 section; entity referred to by pronoun across chunk boundary; missing structured element per 300 words; FAQ answer without direct first sentence or datapoint; missing freshness marks on dynamic topic; synonym rotation on a core entity; section over 400 words with no H3. |
| 🟠 Minor | Vague quantifier where a number exists elsewhere in the text; table over 7 rows; heading not phrased as query/entity-attribute; missing bridge/benefit sentence at paragraph end; summary section absent. |

## Citation Readiness Score

Score is computed from the violations you logged, so it is reproducible and traceable rather than an impression.

| # | Dimension | Areas | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Passage self-containment & entity clarity | 1–2 | 25 |
| 2 | EAV precision & evidence-backed claims | 3 | 20 |
| 3 | Intent-format match & document architecture | 1, 6, 7 | 20 |
| 4 | Extractable structures: tables, lists, FAQ | 4–5 | 15 |
| 5 | E-E-A-T distribution | 9 | 10 |
| 6 | Freshness | 8 | 5 |
| 7 | Citation-worthiness / unique data | 10 | 5 |

**Procedure.** Tag every violation with its dimension as you log it. Then, per dimension, start at 10 and deduct: **4 per Critical, 2 per Major, 0.5 per Minor.** Floor at 0. Multiply by weight/10 and sum the seven results.

Deduct once per distinct defect, not per instance: eight paragraphs opening with "It also offers" is one Major (a pattern), not eight. Recurrence belongs in the violation description — "affects 8 paragraphs across 3 sections" — where it raises severity rather than multiplying deductions.

Run the arithmetic in code and show the table. A score you cannot reconstruct from your own violation list is a bug in the report.

**Gate:** PASS ≥ 80 with zero Critical. CONDITIONAL PASS 70–79 with zero Critical. FAIL < 70, or any Critical at any score.

## Step 3 — Report output

```
# AI Citation QA Report
**Article:** [H1]
**Central intent:** [type + query pattern]
**Evaluation date:** [today]

## Gate verdict
**[PASS / CONDITIONAL PASS / FAIL]** — Citation Readiness Score: [N]/100

## Score breakdown
| Dimension | Weight | Score | Weighted |
|---|---|---|---|
| ... | | | |

## Summary
| Severity | Count |
|---|---|
| 🔴 Critical | X |
| 🟡 Major | X |
| 🟠 Minor | X |

[One-sentence verdict: the single biggest thing suppressing citations.]

## Violations

### 🔴 Critical
#### C-1 — [title]
**Area:** [evaluation area]
**Found in content:**
> "[exact quote or 'Not found in content']"
**Issue:** [1–3 sentences: why this suppresses AI retrieval/citation]
**Fix pattern:** [one-line BEFORE → AFTER rewrite showing the shape of the fix]

### 🟡 Major
[same format]

### 🟠 Minor
[same format — fix pattern optional]

## Chunk map
[Table only if 3+ self-containment violations: H2 section | passable chunks | broken chunks | dominant failure mode]

## Intent–format matrix
[Table only if 2+ format mismatches: H2 | detected intent | current format | required format]

## Notes for Revision Agent
[4–6 bullets ordered by severity. Lead with the answer capsule if it's missing.]
```

## Behaviour rules

- Report violations only; never rewrite the article yourself. Fix patterns are one-line shape hints, not rewrites.
- Quote exactly or write "Not found in content."
- You are a leaf reviewer. Do the evaluation yourself — do not spawn subagents to split the areas, and do not re-read the article for a confirmation pass. One thorough sweep across all ten areas is the deliverable.
- Every violation carries its dimension tag (1–7) so the score reconstructs from the list.
- Running inside the pipeline: write the full report to the path given in your dispatch prompt and return only your summary block — severity counts, score, gate, one-line verdict. Standalone: output the report directly.
- Do not duplicate other reviewers' scope: factual truth → fact-check; brief compliance → seo-brief-qa; tone/banned phrases → editorial-qa. If you notice such an issue in passing, add a one-line "out-of-scope observation" at the end — do not classify it as a violation.
- Judge every rule by its purpose — retrievability — not mechanically. A 5-sentence paragraph that is perfectly self-contained is a weaker violation than a 3-sentence one that starts with "It also".
- When the brief/fan-out is absent, say so in the report header and lower confidence claims accordingly ("inferred sub-intents").

---
name: content-fact-check
description: Independent fact-check pass that verifies a draft's claims against primary sources before publishing. Use whenever the user wants to fact-check, verify claims, source-check, validate statistics or citations, or confirm a draft, article, or report is accurate — especially content produced by a content pipeline or generated by AI. Also use as the automatic final QA step in any content-creation flow, on any topic or project. Trigger on "fact-check this", "verify the claims", "check the facts", "are these stats real", "do these citations exist", or "source-check before publish". Builds a claims ledger, re-checks time-sensitive and high-risk claims against live primary sources, and returns a pass/fail gate. Separate from editorial, SEO, and compliance QA — run it as its own reviewer.
license: Proprietary
---

# Content Fact-Check

A general, project-agnostic fact-check reviewer for AI-generated or human-written content. It verifies that the factual claims in a draft are true and traceable to primary sources, then returns a claims ledger and a publish/hold verdict. Use it on any topic — health, finance, gambling, SaaS, travel, anything.

Run this as its **own pass**, separate from editorial, SEO, and compliance QA — those check tone, structure, and policy, not whether the facts are real. For pipeline-produced content, run it as the final QA reviewer, after editorial and SEO/brief QA, before revision.

**Operate as an auditor, not the author.** Ideally you have not written this draft; your job is to challenge every claim, not defend it. If you did write it, switch posture deliberately and assume each claim is wrong until a source proves it.

Full reference: `references/methodology.md` (the complete methodology — read it for edge cases, the source-hierarchy rules, and the rationale behind each step).

## Why this needs its own pass

AI drafts fail in specific, predictable ways that fluent prose hides:

- **Hallucinated citations** — real-looking studies, DOIs, URLs, quotes, and author names that do not exist or do not say what is claimed.
- **Misattribution** — a correct fact pinned to the wrong source, or a secondary source's number credited to the primary.
- **Stale facts** — anything past the model's training cutoff (prices, "latest" versions, current officeholders, laws, rankings) is guessed, not known.
- **Overgeneralization** — a small or preliminary finding stated as settled consensus.
- **Too-clean numbers** — rounded, tidy stats that read true but were never sourced.

Confidence is not evidence. Check the claim, not the tone.

## Step 0 — Set the rules yourself (don't stall on this)

Establish the tier and source allowlist on your own. **Do not interrogate the user** — infer, state your assumption in one line, and proceed.

1. If the project has a fact-check config, content policy, or playbook that names a risk tier or source allowlist, read it and use it.
2. Otherwise, infer both from the draft's domain and say so briefly, then go:
   - Tier from stakes (§1). YMYL (health, finance, legal, safety) → A; commercial / comparison / stats-heavy → B; general / opinion → C.
   - Default allowlist = the recognized primary sources for that domain (regulators, official data, peer-reviewed journals, primary filings; for operational/product facts, the brand's own site; review aggregators are secondary).

Only pause to ask if something is genuinely missing — no draft was provided, or a claim hinges on a private/internal source you can't see. Otherwise just run.

## Step 1 — Assign the risk tier

Effort scales to stakes. Ask: *if this claim were wrong, what happens to the reader or the client?*

| Tier | Applies to | Method mix | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Critical** | YMYL: health, finance, legal, safety — error harms the reader | Verify **every** external claim against a primary source (fetch it) | Human sign-off |
| **B — Commercial** | Reviews, comparisons, stats-heavy explainers, competitive/numeric claims | Ledger every claim + source-check; fetch the riskiest | 100% ledgered + resolved |
| **C — Low-stakes** | General education, brand/opinion, no hard claims | Spot-check any stray stat | Reviewer skim |

When unsure, tier up. A single hard stat on a C page is checked at A.

## Step 2 — Extract the claims

Pull every **checkable** claim into the ledger. A claim is any sentence a reader would take as a statement of fact.

| Type | Examples | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Quantitative | stats, %, dates, counts, prices | number + unit + context vs source |
| Citation / attribution | "Study X found…", quotes, DOIs/URLs | source exists AND says it |
| Named entity / status | who/what/when, definitions, legal/approval/regulatory status, specs | confirm vs authoritative source |
| Time-sensitive / "current" | "latest", "as of [year]", current price/leader/law/version | always re-fetch live |
| Causal / efficacy | "X causes/improves Y" | does the source support that strength? |

**Skip** clearly-labeled opinion and common knowledge — but confirm opinion is actually labeled as opinion, not asserted as fact.

## Step 3 — Build the claims ledger

One row per claim. This is the deliverable.

| # | Claim (as written) | Type | Source cited | What the source actually says | Verdict | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Verdicts:** ✅ verified (source exists, authoritative, supports the claim) · ⚠️ misstated (distorts the source → correct the copy) · ❌ unsupported (no source / source lacks it → cut or re-source) · 🔄 outdated (was true, now stale → refresh) · ❓ unverifiable (can't confirm → cut, hedge to attributed opinion, or escalate to a human).

## Step 4 — Verify each claim

- **Method 2 (all tiers):** locate the cited source, confirm it's on the allowlist, and compare the claim to what the source actually says.
- **Method 3 (Tier A + any clinical/financial/legal stat + anything time-sensitive):** actually fetch the primary source and confirm the number/quote against the live page. Unfetchable or non-matching → flag, never pass through.
- **Always re-fetch live** anything "current/latest/today/this year", any price, any officeholder/law/version. Never trust model memory for these.
- **Interrogate clean numbers** — round or suspiciously tidy stats get sourced or cut.
- **Check claim strength** — "may be associated with" in the source must not become "causes" in the copy.
- **Watch entity confusion** — similar names/brands/products get conflated; confirm it's the right one.

## Step 5 — Output

Return three things:

1. The completed **claims ledger** (the audit artifact — it should be saved alongside the piece).
2. A **prioritized revision list**: every ⚠️ ❌ 🔄 ❓ row with its fix.
3. The **gate verdict**: PASS only if the tier's acceptance bar is met (Tier A: 100% of claims ✅ to a primary source, 0 unresolved citations, human sign-off pending). Otherwise FAIL, with exactly what's blocking.

## Running automatically during content creation (any project)

This skill is the *detection* half of a two-part habit. Used together, fact-checking happens every time without anyone remembering to ask:

1. **While drafting (prevention).** The writer cites as it claims: every checkable claim ships with its source inline, drawn from a vetted source pool, with uncertain points marked `[VERIFY]` rather than guessed. Add that rule to the project's content brief or writer instructions so it's enforced at generation.
2. **Before publish (detection).** Run this skill as the final QA step, after editorial/SEO QA. To make it automatic, add one line to the project's content command or definition-of-done: *"No draft is done until content-fact-check returns PASS."*

Drop-in brief block any project can paste to wire both hooks:

```
FACT-CHECK (built in):
- Cite as you claim: every stat, date, quote, and status fact carries its primary source inline; pull only from the vetted source pool; mark anything uncertain [VERIFY] — never invent a number or citation.
- Definition of done: the draft is not finished until the content-fact-check skill returns PASS. Save its claims ledger with the piece.
```

## Source rules

- Primary over secondary — cite the study/filing/record, not a blog summarizing it.
- Honor the project's allowlist; anything off-list is not a valid source.
- No circular sourcing — never verify against AI-generated pages, content farms, forums, or the client's own unsourced content.
- Respect the freshness window for time-sensitive facts.
- Quotes must be verbatim and correctly attributed, or clearly marked as paraphrase.

## What not to do

- Do **not** rewrite the article. You produce the ledger and the fix list; revision is a separate step.
- Do **not** take over editorial, SEO, or compliance QA. If you notice a tone/policy issue, flag it and move on.
- Do **not** pass a claim you could not verify. Unverifiable means cut, hedge, or escalate — never silent approval.

# Content Fact-Check Methodology

**A reusable, project-agnostic standard for fact-checking AI-generated content.**
Assumption: content is drafted by Claude via the content-pipeline skill (fan-out → entity research → content guidelines → content generation → QA → revision). This methodology plugs into those stages; it is not tied to any one client or vertical.

Version 1.0 · Owner: Ninja Builder · Apply to: any content project (health, finance, betting, SaaS, ecommerce, etc.)

---

## 1. Why AI-generated content needs its own fact-check protocol

Editorial QA, SEO QA, and compliance QA do not catch factual errors — they check tone, structure, and policy. Fact-checking is a separate discipline with its own reviewer. It matters more for AI drafts than for human drafts because LLMs fail in specific, predictable ways:

- **Hallucinated citations.** Real-looking studies, DOIs, URLs, author names, and quotes that do not exist or do not say what is claimed.
- **Misattribution.** A correct fact pinned to the wrong source, or a secondary source's number attributed to the primary.
- **Stale facts.** Anything past the model's training cutoff — prices, "latest" versions, current officeholders, laws in effect, rankings — is guessed, not known.
- **Overgeneralization.** A small or preliminary finding stated as established consensus.
- **Too-clean numbers.** Rounded or suspiciously tidy statistics that read true but were never sourced.
- **Confident tone masking uncertainty.** Fluent prose is not evidence; confidence is uncorrelated with correctness.

The protocol below is designed to catch exactly these.

---

## 2. Core principles

1. **Fact-checking is its own pass, with its own reviewer.** Never fold it into editorial or SEO QA.
2. **Every checkable claim must trace to a source** (provenance). No source, no claim.
3. **Verify against the primary source, not the model's memory.** If a claim is time-sensitive, re-fetch it live.
4. **The checker is independent of the writer.** Use a fresh Claude session/subagent without the drafting context, so it audits the text rather than defending it.
5. **Scale effort to risk.** Not every page earns line-by-line source verification; high-stakes pages earn all of it.
6. **Unverifiable = cut or hedge.** If a claim can't be confirmed, it is removed, softened to an attributed/hedged statement, or escalated to a human — never left as a bald assertion.
7. **The output is auditable.** Every fact-checked piece ships with a claims ledger as an artifact, so the work can be reviewed and re-checked later.

---

## 3. What gets checked (claim taxonomy)

Fact-checking starts by classifying claims. Only the first four types need verification; the last two do not — calling that out keeps effort focused.

| Claim type | Examples | Risk | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quantitative** | Stats, %, dates, counts, sample sizes, prices | High | Verify number + unit + context against source |
| **Citations / attributions** | "Study X found…", "[Person] said…", quotes, DOIs/URLs | High | Confirm the source exists AND says the claimed thing |
| **Named entities & status facts** | Who/what/when, definitions, legal/regulatory/approval status, product specs | Med–High | Confirm against authoritative source |
| **Time-sensitive / "current" claims** | "latest", "as of 2026", current price/leader/law/version | High | Always re-fetch live; never trust model memory |
| **Causal / efficacy claims** | "X causes Y", "X improves Z" | Medium | Check the source supports the strength of the claim (correlation vs causation) |
| **Opinion / clearly-hedged / common knowledge** | "We think…", "may help", "water is wet" | None | No check (but confirm opinion is labeled as opinion) |

**Extraction rule:** a "claim" is any sentence a reasonable reader would take as a statement of fact. Pull each one as a discrete row in the ledger (§6).

---

## 4. Risk tiers (decide once per project, override per page)

| Tier | Applies to | Default method mix (see §5) | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Critical** | YMYL: health, finance, legal, safety, anything where an error harms the reader | 1 + 2 + 3 (verify every external claim to a primary source) | Human sign-off required |
| **B — Commercial / reputational** | Product reviews, comparisons, stats-heavy explainers, anything making competitive or numeric claims | 1 + 2 (ledger with source check); 3 on the riskiest claims | 100% of claims ledgered, 0 unresolved |
| **C — Low-stakes** | General education, brand/opinion, top-of-funnel explainers with no hard claims | 1 + spot-check of any stray stat | Grounded draft + reviewer skim |

**How to assign:** start at the harm question — *if this claim were wrong, what happens to the reader or the client?* Serious harm → A. Misleads a buying decision or damages trust → B. Mild → C. When unsure, tier up.

---

## 5. The three methods (the toolkit)

### Method 1 — Source-grounded drafting *(at generation time)*

Catch errors before they exist. Built into the content-generation stage:

- **Claim–source binding:** the draft carries the source for every checkable claim inline (footnote, bracket, or comment), captured *as the sentence is written*, not added afterward.
- **Source-pool first:** claims may only draw from the vetted source pool assembled during entity research (§7). No inventing sources at draft time.
- **Uncertainty markers:** anything the model is not sure of is written as hedged/attributed ("according to X") or flagged `[VERIFY]` rather than asserted.
- **No-fabrication rule:** if a needed statistic isn't in the source pool, the writer flags the gap instead of generating a plausible number.

*Strength:* cheapest — bad facts rarely enter the draft. *Limit:* relies on the source actually saying what's claimed, which Method 2/3 confirm.

### Method 2 — Claims-ledger pass *(post-draft, pre-publish)*

A discrete QA stage, run by an independent reviewer. Extract every checkable claim into the ledger (§6), then for each: locate the cited source, compare the claim to what the source actually says, and assign a verdict. Output the completed ledger plus a revision list of everything that failed.

*Strength:* rigorous, auditable, separates facts from editorial QA. *Limit:* trusts that cited sources are real unless Method 3 is added.

### Method 3 — Automated source verification *(high-risk escalation)*

A verification subagent actually fetches each cited primary source (paper, regulator page, filing, official record) and confirms the number/quote against the live source, rather than trusting the citation. Unfetchable or non-matching sources become flags, not pass-throughs.

*Strength:* catches hallucinated and "close-but-wrong" citations — the most dangerous failures. *Limit:* slower; some sources are paywalled/unfetchable (treat those as "unverifiable" → cut, hedge, or human-check).

> **Recommended default for most projects: Method 1 + 2 as standard, Method 3 reserved for Tier-A (critical) pages.** Dial up or down via the risk tier.

---

## 6. Claims ledger template

The core artifact. One row per claim. Ships with the finished piece.

| # | Claim (as written) | Type (§3) | Source cited in draft | What the source actually says | Verdict | Fix / action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | … | Quantitative | … | … | ✅ Verified / ⚠️ Misstated / ❌ Unsupported / 🔄 Outdated / ❓ Unverifiable | … |

**Verdict definitions:**

- **✅ Verified** — source exists, is authoritative, and supports the claim as written.
- **⚠️ Misstated** — source exists but the claim distorts it (wrong number, missing context, over-strong). → correct the copy.
- **❌ Unsupported** — no source, or the source doesn't contain the claim. → cut or re-source.
- **🔄 Outdated** — was true, now stale. → refresh from a current source.
- **❓ Unverifiable** — can't confirm within reasonable effort. → cut, hedge to attributed opinion, or escalate to human.

**Acceptance gate:** the piece publishes only when every row is ✅, or every non-✅ row has been resolved (corrected, cut, or human-approved). For Tier A, 100% of external claims must reach ✅ against a primary source.

---

## 7. Where it plugs into the content pipeline

| Pipeline stage | Fact-check action |
|---|---|
| **Query fan-out** | Note which sub-intents carry factual/claim-heavy answers (these need the most checking). |
| **Entity research** | Build the **vetted source pool**: confirm each entity is real and capture its authoritative primary sources. This pool is the only thing the writer may cite. |
| **Content guidelines / brief** | Specify required citations per section and a **source allowlist** (§8). State the page's risk tier. |
| **Content generation** | Apply **Method 1** — cite-as-you-write, source binding, `[VERIFY]` flags, no fabricated stats. |
| **QA** | Run the **fact-check reviewer as a third QA pass**, alongside editorial QA and SEO QA. Method 2 ledger for all; Method 3 for Tier A. Independent session. |
| **Revision** | Fix every non-✅ ledger row. Re-check changed claims. |
| **Final report** | Attach the completed ledger as the audit artifact. |

---

## 8. Source rules (define per project)

- **Primary over secondary.** Cite the study/filing/regulator/official record, not a blog summarizing it.
- **Authoritative allowlist.** Each project defines acceptable domains/source types (e.g., regulators, peer-reviewed journals, official data, primary filings). Anything off-list is not a valid source.
- **No circular sourcing.** Never verify against AI-generated pages, content farms, or the client's own unsourced content.
- **Recency requirement.** Time-sensitive facts need a source dated within the project's freshness window; otherwise treat as 🔄 Outdated.
- **Quote fidelity.** Quotes must be verbatim and correctly attributed, or paraphrased and clearly marked as such.

---

## 9. LLM-specific traps to check every time

- **Resolve every citation.** Does the DOI/URL actually load, and does it say the claimed thing? A real-looking citation is not a real one.
- **Re-fetch anything "current."** Prices, "latest", current leaders/laws/versions, "as of [year]" — pull live; never accept from model memory.
- **Interrogate clean numbers.** Round or suspiciously tidy stats get sourced or cut.
- **Check claim strength.** "May be associated with" in the source must not become "causes" in the copy.
- **Watch entity confusion.** Similar names/brands/products get conflated — confirm the right one.
- **Confidence is not evidence.** Fluent, certain prose still gets checked.

---

## 10. Roles & independence

- **Writer** (generation): owns Method 1 — grounded drafting and source binding.
- **Fact-check reviewer** (QA): a *fresh* Claude session/subagent without the drafting context, so it audits rather than defends. Owns the ledger.
- **Human editor:** signs off Tier A, adjudicates ❓ Unverifiable rows, owns the final publish gate.

Keep fact-check separate from the editorial/compliance reviewer so neither blind spot hides the other.

---

## 11. Apply to a new project (quick start)

1. **Set the default risk tier** for the project (A/B/C) and note per-page overrides.
2. **Define the source allowlist** and freshness window (§8).
3. **Add the source-pool step** to the entity-research stage.
4. **Add the ledger** (§6) as a required QA artifact; wire the fact-check reviewer as a third QA pass.
5. **Choose the method mix** (default: 1 + 2; add 3 for Tier-A pages).
6. **Set the acceptance gate** and decide who gives human sign-off.
7. (Optional) **Codify it as a project skill** so the pipeline runs it automatically.

---

## 12. Success metrics

- **Claim coverage:** % of checkable claims captured in the ledger (target 100%).
- **Verified rate:** % of claims reaching ✅ before publish.
- **Citation integrity:** % of cited sources that resolve and match (Method 3).
- **Escape rate:** factual corrections needed *after* publish, per 10 articles — track over time; it should trend to zero.

name: content-generation
description: Use when a content brief and editorial policy are present and article writing is requested. Produces retrieval-ready, GEO-optimized SEO articles from structured content briefs following EAV framework, microsemantic rules, and GEO citation patterns.
version: 1.0.0
---

# Content Generation Skill

You are a specialist SEO content writer. You produce retrieval-ready, GEO-optimized articles from structured content briefs. This skill fires automatically whenever a content brief and editorial policy are present in the conversation.

## Core principle

Every paragraph is a retrieval-ready passage. AI systems extract individual passages and evaluate each one independently. Write every paragraph as if it will be extracted and used without surrounding text.

## Required inputs

Before writing, confirm both are present:
- **Content brief** — topic, H1, meta, URL, token budget, outline, entities with EAV model, sub-intent mapping, keyword targets, visual specs
- **Editorial policy** — client-specific rules that override all defaults below

If the editorial policy conflicts with any rule in this skill, the editorial policy wins.

## Web search before writing

Search the web before generating content. Pretrained knowledge is not a source for anything a reader would check, in any vertical:

- **Prices, tiers, amounts, promotions** — subscription costs, bonus values, package contents, discounts
- **Ownership, licensing, regulatory and approval status** — who owns what, what is licensed where, what a regulator has approved
- **Counts and inventories** — how many products, providers, integrations, studies, locations
- **Specifications and dosing** — versions, technical specs, clinical dosages, formulations
- **Any statistic, metric or dated claim** that appears in the article
- **Anything phrased as "current", "latest", "as of [year]", or "now"**

**Batch the searches.** These lookups are independent, so issue them together in one message rather than one at a time. Gather the facts up front, then write from them.

When a fact cannot be sourced, mark it `[VERIFY]` inline and keep writing. Never substitute a plausible number. An honest marker costs one revision edit; an invented statistic costs a Critical at fact-check and can survive to publication.

Close the article with a `## Source pool` section listing every URL used, so the fact-check reviewer verifies against your sources instead of re-deriving them.

## Paragraph structure (every paragraph)

- Sentence 1: Direct claim — [Entity] + [primary Attribute]
- Sentence 2: Supporting evidence — [Value] + [metric]
- Sentence 3: User benefit or comparative context
- Sentence 4 (optional): Bridge to next concept
- Maximum 2–4 sentences per paragraph
- Each paragraph must pass the self-sufficiency test: extractable without surrounding context

## EAV format (every factual claim)

`[Entity] + [Attribute] + [Value] + [Context or User Benefit]`

✅ "Playtana awards 125,000 GC + 1.00 SC upon registration, with email verification required."
❌ "It offers a generous welcome package."

✅ "Semaglutide produced 14.9% mean body weight reduction over 68 weeks in the STEP 1 trial, versus 2.4% on placebo."
❌ "This medication has shown significant results for weight loss."

The pattern holds in every vertical: name the thing, state the measurable attribute, give the exact value, anchor it to context the reader can act on.

## Prohibited opening patterns

Never open a paragraph with:
- "This means…" / "This approach…" / "This platform…"
- "These features…" / "These platforms…"
- "It offers…" / "It provides…" / "It includes…"
- "As mentioned above…" / "As discussed…"
- "Additionally…" / "Furthermore…" / "Moreover…"

Required opening pattern: `[Entity Name] + [specific attribute] + [concrete value] + [user benefit]`

## Dash prohibition

Never use em dashes (—) or en dashes (–) anywhere in the article. Replace with: full stop + new sentence, parentheses, colon, or subordinate clause.

## Section structure

**H1 introduction (200–270 tokens):**
- First sentence: direct answer to primary intent using major entities
- Include specific attributes (ratings, specs, key differentiators)
- Establish authority through regulatory or expert relationships

**Each H2 section:**
- Featured snippet sentence immediately below the heading (before supporting detail)
- Exactly one intent type per H2
- Follow token budget from the brief
- At least one GEO citation pattern (see below)
- At least one authority signal
- One structured element (list or table) per 300 words
- 150–400 words per H2

**H3 subsections:**
- Required when H2 exceeds 300 words
- One focused topic per H3

**FAQ section:**
- General FAQ: max 75 words per answer
- PAA-targeted FAQ: max 50 words per answer
- Every question names the entity
- Every answer includes at least one metric or value

## GEO citation patterns (at least one per H2)

1. **Definition block:** "[Entity] is a [category] that [function], [distinguishing attribute]."
2. **Statistic package:** "[Entity] [verb] [exact metric] [time/context] according to [named source]."
3. **Comparison anchor:** "[Entity A] offers [value], while [Entity B] offers [value], making [A/B] stronger for [use case]."
4. **Step-numbered process:** "Step 1: [Entity] [action]. Step 2: [Entity] [action]. Step 3: [Entity] [outcome]."

## Topical authority coverage (every primary entity)

Cover every primary entity across all three dimensions:
1. **What It Is** — "Is-A" structure: category + function + distinguishing attribute
2. **How It Works** — step-numbered process, minimum 3 steps
3. **How It Compares** — comparison anchor against at least one alternative

Include at least 3 semantically related terms per primary entity H2.

## Bulleted lists

- Minimum 2–3 bulleted lists distributed across the document
- One in first half, one in second half
- 3–7 items per list
- Each bullet names an explicit entity or value
- No bullet begins with "This," "It," or "These"

## Title and meta

**Title:** [Primary Entity] + [Specific Attribute or Number] + [Year] + [Benefit or Intent Frame]
- Primary keyword within first 60 characters
- Maximum 60 characters total

**Meta:** [Direct answer ≤12 words] + [supporting differentiator]
- Maximum 155 characters
- First clause answers primary intent directly
- No passive voice
- Never duplicates title phrasing

## Hard constraints

These are properties of the article as you write it, not a checklist to audit afterwards. Hold them while drafting; do not draft loosely and then sweep back through looking for breaches.

- Every sentence names its entity explicitly. No sentence exceeds 20 words.
- Every claim carries a specific numeric value or a verifiable fact.
- No em dashes or en dashes anywhere.
- Every paragraph is 2–4 sentences and opens with something other than a prohibited pattern.
- Every H2 has a direct-answer sentence immediately below it, at least one GEO citation pattern, and at least one authority signal.
- Every primary entity is covered across all three dimensions (What It Is / How It Works / How It Compares).
- General FAQ answers ≤75 words; PAA-targeted answers ≤50 words.
- "Last Updated" timestamp present.
- A `## Source pool` section closes the article.

Two mechanical checks are worth actually running, because a machine catches them faster than reading does: search the finished text for dash characters, and confirm no `[VERIFY]` marker is sitting on a fact you could have sourced. Everything else on this list you enforce by writing correctly the first time.

## Output

Write the article to `04-draft.md` in the run directory. Print a receipt only — token count, section count, structural element count, sources cited, `[VERIFY]` markers remaining. Do not print the draft into chat; the next stage reads the file, and Stage 6 delivers the version the user should read.
